I spent most of this morning testing the local dictation app on my laptop, and I want to leave a memo while the details are fresh. The app is called ScribeNest, and I installed the current desktop build from the project page on Friday. I am using it on a ThinkPad with Windows 11 and a USB-C dock, but I unplugged the dock for some of the tests because I wanted to see whether the behavior changed without the external screen and keyboard. I was not trying to benchmark it in a controlled way; these are just the things I noticed while using it for ordinary notes and a couple of longer passages.

1. The hotkeys are mostly easy to remember. Ctrl+Shift+Space starts dictation, and the same combination stops it, at least that is what the quick-start card says. The first time I tried it, I had the Notes window focused, and it started correctly. The little toast said “Listening.” Then I spoke two sentences and pressed the keys again. It stopped and put the words in the note. When I switched to my browser, the shortcut still worked there too, but on one try it inserted a space into the browser page before the app took focus. I may have pressed the keys unevenly, or the browser might have handled part of the combination. I could not make that happen again. The separate shortcut for pausing is Ctrl+Shift+P, and that one was less convenient because my left hand was already near the space bar. I changed the pause shortcut in settings to Alt+Shift+P, and the setting stayed after I quit and reopened ScribeNest.

2. Microphone selection. The first run picked the built-in microphone automatically, even though my USB headset was plugged in. I opened audio settings and chose “Headset Microphone (USB Audio Device),” which is the name Windows showed me. The input meter moved when I spoke, and the built-in mic meter did not appear at the same time. After I unplugged the headset, ScribeNest switched to the laptop microphone without showing a warning. I plugged the headset back in, and it kept using the laptop microphone until I selected the headset again. So it seems like unplugging the selected device changes the choice, but plugging it back in does not necessarily restore it. I have not checked whether that depends on the order in which the devices are connected. The settings page also has a noise reduction switch, and I left it off because I was mainly watching the device behavior rather than comparing sound quality.

3. Tray status. The icon stays in the system tray when the main window is closed, and its little microphone mark is gray when it is idle. While recording, it turns green. The green mark was useful because the main window was behind other windows for part of the test. If I right-click the tray icon, there are choices for Start Dictation, Open History, and Quit. I first assumed the X on the window would quit the app, but it only hid the window in the tray. I had to use Quit from the tray menu to close it fully. I found that once because the keyboard shortcut did nothing after I thought I had closed the app, but it had actually remained open. There is also a small dot on the icon when a transcription is waiting to be inserted. I did not see any explanation for that dot in the quick-start card, but it went away when I clicked back into the note.

4. Language detection. I left Language on Automatic for a short note in English, and it selected English correctly. For the longer test, it also labeled the passage as English, but it took a little longer before the text appeared. The app offers English, Spanish, and German in the menu, and there is a choice to keep one language selected instead of Automatic. I did not test a full passage in another language, so I cannot say how reliable that part is. I did say one Spanish street name inside an English sentence, and the app wrote a close-sounding English phrase rather than the name I had expected. That could be the pronunciation, or the language setting, or the model. I did not repeat that word enough to tell. I switched Automatic off and selected English before the next passage, and the rest of the English words looked about the same to me.

5. Saved history. I found the History page from the tray menu, and it showed the date and the first few words of each test. It kept the short note and the longer passage after I closed the note app and restarted ScribeNest. I opened one history entry, and there was a Copy button and a Delete button. I copied the short entry into a blank file, and the text matched what I remembered dictating. I did not delete anything because I wanted to check whether the list stayed in order. The page had a search box, but I only searched for a word that was already visible in one entry, and it narrowed the list. I could not find a setting that says how long entries remain saved, and I do not know whether the history is stored only on this computer or somewhere else. The app was offline during this part, but I had connected the laptop earlier in the morning.

6. Accidental activation. This was the part I was most concerned about because the shortcut is easy to hit while my fingers are near the keys. During the test, I accidentally started listening once while I was trying to switch windows, and the green tray icon made me notice it before I said anything private. I pressed the shortcut again, and it stopped without creating text, as far as I could see. Another time, I had a podcast playing quietly and tapped the hotkey while reaching for the space bar. The app stayed listening until I noticed the icon and stopped it. I do not know if any audio from that short interval was saved because there was no new history item and no message on screen. I found an option called “Confirm before recording” and turned it on. After that, a small box appeared asking whether to start. I left it enabled for the rest of the test. It adds one click, but it seems easier to notice than relying on the tray icon alone.

7. Error messages. I unplugged the headset while the app was listening to see what it would do. The tray icon flashed red, and a box said, “Input device unavailable. Select another microphone to continue.” I selected the laptop mic, and dictation resumed after a short pause. It did not fill in the words from the moment when the device was disconnected. At another point, I clicked Start when no microphone permission had been granted yet, and Windows showed a permission prompt before the app displayed, “Microphone access is blocked. Check privacy settings.” That wording was direct, but the privacy settings link opened the general microphone page, not the app-specific entry. I had to scroll down to find ScribeNest in the list. I allowed access, then reopened the app, and the microphone worked. I did not see a crash or a long technical error code in either case.

8. Clipboard ownership. I copied text from History and then copied a sentence from a web page to check whether the app kept controlling the clipboard after the copy action. The web page sentence replaced the history text, as expected. When I used the Insert command from the recording window, it pasted the transcription into the active note, and then another copy command in the note replaced it. I did not see a clipboard manager or a notice that ScribeNest had kept an old copy around. There is a setting called “Copy completed text automatically,” and it was off by default. I turned it on for one test. The transcript appeared in the note and was also available when I pasted into a second blank file. I turned the option off again afterward because I do not always want a new transcript replacing something I copied for another task.

9. Offline use. I turned off Wi-Fi and opened a fresh note after checking that the app was still running. The tray menu remained available, and a short English sentence appeared without a connection. I then tried a longer paragraph, and that also produced text. The settings page showed a small offline label beside the selected English model. I had downloaded that model during installation, so the test does not tell me what happens before a model is present. I turned Wi-Fi back on after a few minutes and did not notice any difference in the words from the next short note. The history entry from the offline test appeared in the same list. I did not sign out or switch networks, and I did not test whether updates or language downloads work offline.

10. Latency impressions. On the short notes, the text usually began to appear while I was still speaking or within a moment after I stopped. There was one pause of several seconds after the longer passage, and the tray icon stayed green during that time. I am describing how it felt rather than measuring it with a timer. The pauses seemed more noticeable when I used the laptop microphone from farther away, but I also spoke more slowly in that part of the test, so I would not treat that as a comparison. The history entry was available shortly after the text appeared, and I did not notice the app freezing. The typing cursor in the note moved to the end when the text was inserted, which was convenient, but I have not checked how it handles a note where the cursor is in the middle of an existing paragraph.

11. Installation. I downloaded the Windows installer from the project page, and Windows asked me to confirm that I wanted to run it. I did not get the application through the Microsoft Store. The installer asked where to put the program and whether to create a desktop shortcut. I accepted the default folder and left the shortcut box checked. The install finished without asking me to restart the laptop. At first launch, it asked for microphone permission and then offered the English model download. I had a connection for that part, and the download bar moved steadily, though I did not time it. The app appeared in the Start menu and in Add or Remove Programs after installation. I had to open settings myself to allow it through the microphone privacy page. The installer did not appear to change my browser or add any other obvious program. I have not tried to uninstall it or install a newer build over this one, and if I try

I went out to the little solar installation on Thursday morning with Leah from facilities. We got there a little after eight. The site is behind the east end of the community workshop, not on the workshop roof itself. It is a separate low building with a metal roof. The forecast had said showers later, but when we arrived it was bright and cold, and the roof was dry. I could see a line of cloud coming in from the south, but I don't know whether that had anything to do with the output readings later on. The visit was mainly to look at the panels and the inverter and get a sense of what the maintenance records showed, not to make any changes to the equipment.

From the ground, the array looked tidy at first. There are twelve panels in two rows, and I counted six in each row. The row nearer the fence is shaded at the left end by a large maple tree. The shadow was across part of the first panel and a narrow strip of the second panel at 8:27. I didn't measure the length of the shadow, and I can't say how much of either panel was shaded; that was just what I could see from below. The upper row looked clear from that angle, although I could not see the far edge of every panel. We walked around the east and south sides, and there were no branches touching the roof. Leah said the tree is on the neighbor's property, but I didn't check that, and I'm not sure who could arrange pruning if that becomes necessary.

We did not climb onto the roof. There is a ladder fixed to the west wall, but there was a chain across the access area and a sign on it that says, "AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY." Leah said roof access has to be arranged through the building manager and that she did not have the key to the chain with her. We stayed on the ground and did not move the chain or use the ladder. From where we stood, I could see a conduit going up the wall and disappearing over the roof edge, but not the fittings at the top. I did not see any obvious broken glass or loose panel edges from the ground. That is not a full inspection of the roof.

At the inverter cabinet, the outer door was closed, and the cabinet was mounted on the north wall inside the fenced service area. The fence gate was open when we arrived, and Leah closed it behind us. There is a yellow painted line on the concrete around the cabinet. She said to stay outside that line unless the electrical technician is present. We stayed outside it. I did not open the cabinet or touch any switches. The display could be read through the small window. At 9:12, it showed a total energy reading of 1842 kilowatt-hours and a daily reading of 3.6 kilowatt-hours. I may have misread the last digit on the daily number because the display was faint, but I'm fairly sure it was 3.6. The time shown on the display was 9:08, which was four minutes behind my phone.

There were two alert entries visible on the inverter screen. One said “grid voltage high” with a time of 7:14, and the other said “communication interrupted” with a time of 7:16. Both were marked as cleared on the display. I copied those words into my notebook and did not take a screenshot. The display didn't show how long either alert had lasted, and I don't know whether they were related to one another. Leah thought the communication alert might be from the monitoring connection dropping out overnight, but she said that was a guess, not something she had confirmed. She also wondered if the high-voltage alert could happen when demand on the local line is low, but neither of us checked any network information while we were there.

I looked at the visible cable runs around the side of the building. There are labels on three of the cables beside the inverter, and I read them as PV A, PV B, and data. The first two labels are white wraparound tags, and the data label is blue. There was another cable running down the wall toward a small gray box, but I could not see a label on it from where I was standing. I started to say that cable was unlabeled, but I should say I could not see a label because the back side was turned toward the wall. I didn't trace any of the cables, and I can't tell where the gray box connects. The tags looked legible from a short distance, though the lettering on PV B was faded at the edge.

Leah said the workshop facilities team handles clearing leaves near the building and arranging general access, but the solar equipment itself is covered by a service agreement with Northline Electrical. She thought the agreement was renewed last spring, or maybe the spring before, and said she would need to check the paperwork. She was not sure if Northline is responsible for the panels as well as the inverter, or only the inverter and electrical connections. Nobody had contacted the contractor for this visit, and we did not ask them to attend. Leah said there used to be a monthly visual check, but she did not know if that was still being done. I didn't find a current checklist in the folder she brought, and she said maintenance responsibility for the tree was not clear to her.

The folder was a thin blue binder kept in the workshop office. It had an old installation plan and a one-page handover sheet, but I did not find a roof layout showing the panel serial numbers. There was also no recent inverter export or record of the alert entries that I could see. The handover sheet had a date of 18 June 2021 and a name at the bottom, but no phone number. The installation plan was folded, and some of the writing was too small to read in the office light. Leah said the electronic records may be held by the building manager or by Northline, but she did not know which. I didn't look through the manager's files, and I haven't seen the service agreement, so I can't confirm the renewal date or exactly what the contract covers.

By about 10:30, it had clouded over, and there was a light shower as we were walking back to the workshop. The roof was still visible from the path, but I did not go back to check for water or inspect the panels during the rain. I don't know whether the shower was heavy enough to affect the system, and I did not compare the daily reading with a sunny-day reading. No water was dripping from the inverter cabinet that I could see from outside, and the ground beside it was damp by then. That might simply have been rain coming across the open area. I didn't see water entering the cabinet or any pooling against the wall.

Leah's work mobile is 07700 900 614, and she gave me the email address leah dot morris at eastbank workshop dot org. I wrote both down while we were in the office. She said the building manager is called Daniel Price and that he is usually on site on Monday and Wednesday mornings. I do not have his direct number or email, and she didn't want to guess them. She offered to send a message asking him to confirm the roof access arrangement and where the maintenance records are kept. I haven't received that confirmation yet. The service contractor contact she had in her phone was saved as Northline service desk, but she did not read out a number, and I didn't ask her to search for one while we were there.

For follow-up, I think we need to confirm who can authorize roof access before anyone plans a closer look at the shading or panel condition. We should ask for the current service agreement and find out who records the inverter alerts and whether the monthly visual checks are still happening. Those are questions, not findings from this visit. The team may also need some basic training on what the display readings mean and what staff should do when an alert appears. Leah said she would be comfortable with a short walkthrough, but she wasn't asking to operate the inverter by herself. I haven't arranged a training session, and I don't know who would provide it. It might be Northline if they are still under contract, or it might need to be arranged through the building manager.

My main notes, then, are partial shading at the fence end of the lower row as seen from the ground; visible labels on three cable runs; two cleared alerts on the display; and a daily reading I believe was 3.6 kilowatt-hours. There are limits to all of those observations because I didn't access the roof, open the cabinet, trace cables, or verify the records. The possible cause of the alerts and the responsibility for the tree are both uncertain. I left the equipment as I found it and did not make any changes. The next useful step is to get the access and maintenance information and then decide whether a qualified person needs to inspect anything more closely.

So this is the voice memo about what we need for the neighborhood repair cafe, and I want to get the requirements down before we book a room. The point is to help neighbors look at ordinary broken household things and learn what might be repairable. It is not a promise that every item can be fixed, and it is not a place where people leave something and come back later expecting it to be ready. We need a simple welcome table, an intake sheet, and a way to explain the limits before anybody gets in the queue.

For the intake categories: first, small furniture and household fittings, like a loose chair leg or a drawer that sticks; second, clothing and textiles, like a torn seam or a bag strap; third, bicycles and their small mechanical parts; and fourth, small non-electrical household objects, such as a kettle handle with no wiring involved. Leave small appliances off the first category list until we have the right people. The form should ask what the item is, what the problem is, and whether the person has tried anything already. It should also ask whether there are sharp edges, leaks, broken glass, or anything else the volunteers need to know before picking it up.

We should not ask for a long story or make someone explain why they cannot replace an object. A short description is enough. There should be a separate place for the visitor to mark whether they want to watch and learn, want to try a step themselves, or would rather let the volunteer examine it first. We need to make clear that the owner stays with the item unless there is an agreed reason to move it for a short inspection. If there is a disagreement about a proposed repair, we stop and talk rather than carry on because a volunteer thinks the fix is obvious.

Tool access needs a clear boundary. Visitors can use a hand tool when a volunteer has shown them how and is staying close by, but tools should not be left spread across the room for general use. We need a check-in and check-out list for shared tools, especially the sharp ones and the cordless drill. The drill needs the right bit, and an adult volunteer should be beside anyone who has not used it before. No one should be pressured to handle a tool just because they came to learn. They can watch instead, and that still counts as taking part.

For electrical work, we need to be quite conservative. The cafe is not a testing service, and we should not open mains-powered equipment unless a suitably trained volunteer has agreed in advance to take that particular job. Even then, there should be no live work, and the item must be unplugged before anybody inspects it. We are not going to diagnose wiring by guesswork, and we are not going to tell a visitor that an appliance is safe to use just because it switched on once. If we cannot assess it within our limits, we explain that clearly and suggest they seek a qualified repairer rather than trying another step at the table.

Consent has to be part of every repair, not a formality at the entrance. The volunteer should describe the proposed step and ask before cutting, drilling, opening a casing, or removing a part. The visitor can say no or change their mind, and the repair stops there. If the item belongs to someone else, the person who brought it needs to confirm they are allowed to ask for work on it. We should not take a repair as permission to make a different change, even if the volunteer thinks the change would help.

Photos need their own consent, too. We can ask whether a visitor is happy for a picture of the item to be used in a repair note, but the answer must be optional and should not affect their place in line. No faces or names in those pictures unless the person has separately agreed to that and we have a clear reason to include them. If someone says no, we simply do not take the photo. The repair notes should not include personal details that are not needed to describe the fault and the possible next step.

Queue fairness matters because some repairs take five minutes and some may take most of an afternoon. We should use a visible numbered queue and explain that the number is the order of arrival, not a promise about when a volunteer will be free. We can group jobs by the type of skill needed if that keeps the work moving, but we should not quietly move a friend ahead or give preference to whoever asks most loudly. A quick safety check can happen early when there is a concern, while the full repair stays in its place in line. If somebody has to leave, we can note that they left and explain what options remain rather than guarantee their turn will be held.

Translation should be arranged as part of planning, not improvised after a visitor has arrived. We can ask local community groups which languages are likely to be useful and prepare a short explanation of the process in those languages. We should not treat a child as the default interpreter for a parent if a trained adult interpreter can be arranged, and we need to check with the visitor that they are comfortable with the person translating technical details. Volunteers should use plain words, point to the relevant part, and pause to let people ask questions rather than assume that a nod means they understood.

The room also needs accessible tables and a route between them with no boxes or bags left in the way. At least one work surface should have enough clear space and a height that works for someone who uses a wheelchair, and chairs should be available for people who need to sit while they wait or work. We should avoid putting the sign-in sheet on a high shelf and make sure the queue can be seen without blocking the entrance. We need to ask the venue what access is available at the door and whether there is an accessible toilet nearby, and then tell visitors what we know rather than guess.

Spare parts are another limit. We need small common items like assorted screws, washers, thread, patches, glue, and a few standard bicycle tubes, but we cannot stock every brand or model. We should label donations and check them before putting them in the parts boxes. No one should fit an unknown screw just because it seems close. The owner should hear if a part is being used and whether there is any cost, although the plan is to start with donated parts at no charge. We should keep a note of what we use so we can see what needs replacing and ask local shops about suitable donations without promising they will provide them.

Volunteer training needs to include a welcome and intake practice, safe hand tool use, consent, queue handling, and how to say that a job is outside our skills. People should know where the first aid kit and exit are and who is coordinating the session. A new volunteer can shadow someone experienced before taking a repair on their own, and it is fine to say, “I do not know,” or, “Let me check with the coordinator.” We should not call someone an expert just because they have fixed a similar object at home, and nobody should work beyond the ability they can honestly describe.

For hours, we should open at ten thirty in the morning and plan to finish at one thirty on the first Saturday of each month. That gives us time to set up the tools and have a short briefing before visitors arrive. We need the last intake time to be clear, perhaps twelve thirty, so we can tell people honestly whether there is time to look at their item. The room booking should include setup and cleanup time, and someone needs to check whether the venue has a key or a caretaker on site. If we cannot confirm the room booking, we should not advertise a date as settled.

What we cannot promise is a repair, a particular waiting time, a replacement part, a free service forever, or that an item will be safe after we have looked at it. We can offer a careful conversation and a chance to learn where that is appropriate. We can explain when a job needs specialist equipment or a qualified professional, and we can give the visitor their item back with no change if that is the safest choice. I think that boundary needs to be on the welcome sign and repeated when someone checks in so the cafe feels welcoming without suggesting we can do more than we actually can.

I want to give a review of my train journey from York to Bristol on Sunday the 14th of April because I have limited mobility and use a folding rollator, and I need a little extra time getting on and off trains. I booked about five weeks ahead through the rail company website and added assistance for York and for the change at Birmingham New Street. I asked to have help with the steps and with finding the right platform, but I can manage my own rollator and bags if there is enough room. I also selected a seat near an accessible toilet and asked for an aisle seat because I cannot get past people easily.

When the booking confirmation came, there was an assistance note, but the seat was in coach C by the window. I phoned the number on the confirmation, and the person I spoke to was courteous and said the seat request was recorded but they could not promise the exact seat. I asked whether the coach had space for the rollator and was told there was a luggage area at the end of the carriage. I took that to mean it would be easy to reach from my seat, which it was not. I printed the tickets at home and checked the journey again the night before the trip. The train was shown as leaving York at 8:42, and the connection at Birmingham was scheduled for 24 minutes.

At York, I arrived 35 minutes early and went to the assistance desk. The staff member checked my booking and said someone would meet me at the platform. I asked if they could tell me where the accessible toilet was, and they pointed it out in the station. I used it before boarding, and there was enough time. The platform changed from platform 5 to platform 3 about ten minutes before departure. The change appeared on the screen first and then was announced over the speakers. The announcement was clear, but it came while I was walking slowly toward platform 5. I had to turn around and ask a member of staff which route had a lift. They said to go back along the concourse and use the lift by the ticket office. That was correct, though it took several minutes.

No one was waiting with assistance at platform 3 when I got there. I asked a conductor near the train, and they checked the list and said my assistance had been noted but they had not been told I was there. The conductor helped me step up and put my rollator in the luggage area at the end of coach C. I could not reach it from my seat without moving through the narrow aisle and asking another passenger to stand up. I chose to keep my small bag with me and put my coat on the empty seat beside me until the train filled up. The window seat was the only seat assigned to me, and there was no aisle seat available when I asked onboard.

The train left York about twelve minutes late. The announcement said there was a signal problem outside Leeds and that they would update us when they knew more. I appreciated hearing that because the delay was not explained on the display in my coach. The seats were clean and the heating was comfortable, but the space between the rows felt tight with my knees and the rollator in mind. I asked the conductor if they could help me get my rollator out before Birmingham. They said they would come back when we were closer, but they did not come back. I went to the toilet once during the journey. It was accessible and clean, although the door was heavy and the call button was positioned high for me. I could use it, but someone with less reach might find that difficult.

A few announcements were made about the delay and the connection at Birmingham. The first one said passengers for Bristol should speak to staff on arrival. The later announcement said our arrival time was still uncertain. I could hear both announcements, but some words were masked by noise from the carriage, and I could not see a journey update on the screen over my seat. A passenger across the aisle told me the train was expected to reach Birmingham at 10:16. I asked a member of staff passing through whether assistance had been arranged at the other end, and they said they could not see that information on their handheld device but advised me to wait near the doors when we arrived.

We reached Birmingham New Street at 10:19, and my connection was due to leave at 10:06, so it had already gone. I had been told that assistance would help me change platforms, but there was no staff member waiting by the doors. I stayed on the train until the conductor helped me take out the rollator, and then I asked a station employee where to go. The employee was kind and walked with me to the customer information point. They explained that the next direct train to Bristol was at 11:42 and showed me a lift route to the platform. I had to wait more than an hour in the station. I found a seat near the information point and used the accessible toilet there before boarding again.

I asked at the information point whether the missed connection meant I could claim the cost of a meal or any other expense, and the person said they could not confirm that and gave me a link for making a claim. I later submitted a refund request for the unused part of my ticket and the extra costs I had listed. I have not received a refund, and no refund has been granted so far. I also requested a review of the assistance arrangements and included the platform change and the lack of anyone waiting at Birmingham. I have had an acknowledgement of the request but not a decision. I do not want to suggest that a refund is certain, and I am only describing what has happened to me.

Staff members were polite when I could find them, and the employee who walked me to the information point was particularly helpful. I was less satisfied with how the assistance booking worked in practice. The note on my booking did not seem to ensure that somebody met me after the platform change at York or at the connection in Birmingham. I do not know whether the late-running train caused the assistance problem, but it made the short connection impossible for me to manage independently. The luggage area at the end of the coach was also a problem because I could not retrieve my rollator easily from the seat I had been assigned.

My three recommendations are:
1. Give clearer updates when a platform changes and allow enough time for passengers with mobility needs to use the lift.
2. Make sure assistance staff know when a passenger has arrived and tell the passenger where they will meet them.
3. Consider the position of luggage spaces when assigning seats to people who travel with a rollator.

I would also like the toilet call button to be reachable from a seated position. On this journey, the staff I spoke to were generally kind, but I think the booking and handover arrangements need to be more reliable. These are my personal views based on this trip, and another passenger may have had a different experience.

I have been on the platform team for just over a week, and I wanted to talk through what onboarding has actually been like. A few things are clear now, and a few things are still pretty uncertain. I joined on Tuesday, the sixth of May, and my manager, Lena, introduced me in the team channel and sent me a short list of people to contact. I thought I would spend the first day reading, but most of it was getting access sorted and figuring out which instructions were current. The welcome page says to start with the new starter checklist, but the link goes to a page that was last updated in October, and some of the names on it have moved teams.

First, the access requests. I filed the standard request for the source repository and the internal package registry on Tuesday morning. The repository appeared later that day, but the package registry took until Friday. I could see the package names before I had permission to download anything, and I was not sure if that was expected. I asked in the onboarding channel and got a reply from Nikhil saying access usually takes a day or two, but he was not sure about this particular registry. I also requested the staging dashboard and the service logs, but the form asks for a cost center, and I do not know which one the platform team uses. My manager told me to leave it blank and ask the service owner. I have not heard back from the service owner yet, so those two requests are still open. I can do most of the work without the dashboard right now, but I cannot check whether my local changes match what staging is running.

Second, the documentation is useful once I find it, but there are several routes into the same subject. The setup page points to the old handbook, the handbook points to a runbook, and the runbook assumes I already know how the deployment labels are chosen. There is a newer page called Release Flow, but it does not say who owns it. I think the material has grown over time rather than being deliberately arranged that way. The examples are mostly helpful, especially the section that shows how to run one service locally, but one command in that section uses an environment variable that is not listed there. I found the variable mentioned in a comment on a pull request from last year. I may have missed a newer explanation, if there is one. I would like to know which page people treat as authoritative before I start changing links in the docs.

Lena paired me with Marcos on Wednesday afternoon and with Jo on Thursday morning. Those were both useful sessions. Marcos walked through the request router and showed me where the team keeps small operational scripts. He did not have time to explain the alert rules and said that would probably make more sense when I have access to the staging dashboard. Jo helped me run the test suite and explained how the mock data is loaded. I was about to ask her to review my setup changes when I remembered the team prefers pairing for first-time changes, so we looked at the config together instead. There is a pairing slot on the calendar every afternoon, but I do not know whether people expect newcomers to book it or whether a mentor normally invites them. Jo said either is fine, though she might have meant for this week only. I have been trying not to treat every available calendar block as an invitation.

Code review customs are another thing I am learning gradually. People usually ask for review in the team channel and put the service name in the message, but I have also seen reviews requested directly from one person. The contribution guide says two approvals are required for changes under shared libraries, and one approval is enough for service-specific changes. I have not found a clear rule for edits to deployment configuration. My first small pull request changed a default timeout in a test fixture, and Marcos left one question about whether the value should match the client timeout. He did not approve it yet, and I have not changed the value because I want to understand the reason for the difference first. Someone else added a thumbs-up, but I do not know whether that counts as a review. I asked Lena if I should wait for the designated reviewer or just answer the comment, and she said, “Answer the comment first, then request whoever owns the area.” I am not sure if that applies to every repository or only this one.

Build setup took longer than I expected. The local instructions say to use the container script and then run `make check`, but on my laptop the container started and exited before it printed a clear error. I tried again with the verbose flag and saw that it could not find the internal certificate. I had not yet received the certificate because its access request is separate from repository access. Once that came through on Thursday, the container started normally. The full test command took about twenty-five minutes and failed two tests that depend on a local database. I had not started the database because the setup page says the container starts it automatically. I asked in the channel, and Jo pointed me to a newer compose file that is not linked from the setup page. Using that file fixed the database issue, but I have not rerun the full suite yet. I did run the targeted tests for the router, and those passed. I would like to know if people normally run the full suite before every draft review or wait until the change is close to ready.

There is also a security approval step that I do not understand completely. Before I can request production access, the form asks for the name of a security contact and whether my work will handle customer data. My work might touch identifiers in logs, but I do not know yet whether that counts as customer data. I asked the security channel and received an automated link to the policy. The policy says to contact the security partner for the owning service, but I do not know who that is for the request router. I have not submitted the production access form because I do not want to guess at those answers. Lena said we can identify the right contact in our one-to-one on Monday, so I am waiting for that conversation. I also have not been told whether production access is part of my role or only needed later if I take an on-call shift.

Meeting overlap has been manageable, but it is worth mentioning. My working hours are usually nine to five thirty Eastern, and the platform team has a recurring architecture meeting at eight thirty on Thursdays. I joined this week because the invitation looked important, but I can only make that time occasionally without shifting other commitments. The meeting recording was not available, and the notes only include the decisions, so I missed some context about why the queue migration is planned for June. I am not asking for the meeting to move; I just want to know whether attendance is expected for someone in my role and whether there is a summary or a person I should check with when I cannot attend. The rest of the team meetings are mostly within my hours. There is a project sync on Friday that overlaps with a support handoff by fifteen minutes, and I have not worked out whether those are both essential yet.

One small misunderstanding was the acronym RFC. I thought people meant a request for change because that was how I had seen it used at my previous job, but here they mean request for comments. When someone says there is an RFC open, they are usually asking the team to review a design proposal, not saying that a change has already been approved. I got that wrong in the channel and asked if the rollout was scheduled. Nikhil clarified it without making a big deal of it, and the proposal is still under discussion. There has not been a decision about the rollout yet. Another thing I am trying to keep straight is where my role ends. For now, I have been asked to learn the request router and improve its onboarding notes. I have not been asked to own the service or approve production changes. I can suggest fixes and ask questions, but I do not want to imply that I am responsible for the deployment plan.

There are a few unanswered questions I have written down:
1. Who owns the Release Flow page, and which setup instructions are current?
2. Which cost center should go on the dashboard and logs requests?
3. Who is the security partner for the request router, and is production access expected in my first month?
4. How should I handle reviews when the contribution guide does not cover a particular kind of change?
5. Should I plan to attend the early architecture meeting every week, or only when the agenda concerns work I am doing?

Some of those might be easy to answer in the team channel, but I did not want to send five separate messages while people were busy with the release this week.

For next week, I was thinking of making a small first-week checklist, even though technically it will be my second week now. I would put the access requests and their owners at the top, then the current setup links and the command for starting the local database. After that, the pairing sessions and the people who explained each area, then the review rules and any gaps that still need an answer, and finally the meeting expectations and security contact information. I would keep the checklist in the team onboarding folder rather than my personal notes, but I want to ask before adding another page because that folder already has several overlapping guides. The goal would be to make it easier for the next person to tell what is done, what is blocked, and who can answer the next question, not to create a new official process. I could show a draft to Lena and Jo before sharing it more widely if they think it would be useful. I am not sure whether to start by collecting information from the service owners or first ask the team which existing page should be updated.

I want to give a review of the shared workspace at Harbor House after using it for about four months, on and off, for client work and a weekly planning day. The booking system is mostly straightforward. You can see the small rooms and desks in one calendar, and the confirmation arrives quickly. But the calendar does not show whether a room has a working screen until you open the listing and read the notes. I booked Cedar twice for calls, and once it had a cable and once it did not, so that detail should be visible before payment. The desk bookings are easier because the floor map marks which desks face the windows.

The lighting is good near the south windows in the morning and quite harsh in the central row after two in the afternoon. The lamps above desks 18 through 24 seem much brighter than the rest of the floor, and there is no local switch. I asked at reception and was told facilities could adjust them, but I have not noticed a change. The phone booths have softer lighting, which is better for video calls, though the one by the kitchen has a flickering bulb. I reported that last month, and it is still flickering. Noise changes a lot over the day: quietest before nine and busiest around lunch. The open desk area carries conversations from the kitchen and the front door. The booths help, but sound leaks through their lower door gaps.

Access has been reliable for me during staffed hours. The app code usually works on the first try, and the front desk can print a day pass for a guest. But one Friday I arrived at seven twenty, and the code flashed red twice. I was about to call the number on the door when another member let me in. The help number did not answer until seven thirty-five. I understand that early access may be limited, but the app should say that before someone books an early slot. The lift is slow, but it works, and the accessible entrance is clearly signed. The side gate is harder to find after dark because the small sign is behind a planter.

Storage is enough for a normal day, but not for someone carrying equipment. There are a few open cubbies beside reception and lockers on the lower floor. The lockers need a personal padlock, which is mentioned in the welcome email but not on the booking page. I had to carry a camera bag through two meetings because every locker I checked was occupied. People seem to use some of them for several days at a time. A posted limit or a small number of day-use lockers would help. The kitchen has cups, plates, and a refrigerator, and it is generally clean in the morning. By late afternoon, the counter collects mugs and delivery boxes. I have seen staff clear it, but not on a predictable schedule.

Guests are easy to register if they arrive with me, and the front desk checks their names against the list. However, the guest link is confusing on a phone, and my colleague once completed the form without seeing the field for the date she turned up. The following week, she arrived and the pass had expired. Reception sorted it out after a few minutes, but she had to wait in the lobby. I would also like the guest instructions to say whether visitors may use the kitchen and lounge, because different staff members have given me different answers. The lounge itself is comfortable and useful for a short meeting, but the soft chairs are too low for laptop work.

Printing is convenient for ordinary documents. The printer accepts uploads from a laptop, and the charge appears in the account straight away. The instructions for duplex printing are hidden behind a small help icon, and the machine has twice kept my job in the queue after showing a paper warning, even though the tray was full. I printed a twenty-page proposal and had to send the job again, which meant checking carefully that it had not produced two copies. Color printing is noticeably expensive, but the price is listed clearly. The scanner works well and sends a PDF by email. The room temperature is less consistent: the north meeting room is chilly in the morning, while the center of the open floor gets stuffy after lunch.

I have a personal reason for noticing the temperature and noise, because last November I brought my father here while our flat was being repaired. He had recently started using a folding cane, and I needed to finish a proposal while he waited for a home repair appointment. I booked a small room, thinking it would give us a quiet hour, but the room was cold and the heater control had no label. He sat by the glass wall in his coat while I tried to take a call in the booth next door. Later, he told me that at least the coffee was good and he could watch the buses from the window. That sounds like a small thing, but it made a stressful morning manageable. I should add that a staff member found us a warm blanket without being asked and showed my father the step-free route to the lift. I appreciated that very much.

Late arrival is another area where a little more clarity would help. If a train is delayed, the booking still begins at the original time, and the app does not offer a way to say that I will be twenty minutes late. I once messaged the reception address and got a reply after I had arrived. If the room is still free, no one seems to mind, but I cannot tell whether the charge changes or whether the room might be released for someone else. Cancellation is similarly unclear. A desk can be cancelled in the app, but the rule for meeting rooms appears only in the email receipt. I cancelled Cedar the day before a meeting and received no charge, but the confirmation screen did not say whether that was because I was within a free period or because the payment had not gone through.

Privacy matters when people are taking calls. The booths are useful, but the glass fronts face the main walkway, and people passing can read a screen if the laptop is angled toward the door. The meeting rooms have blinds, though one in Cedar sticks halfway down. I tend to use headphones and avoid leaving papers out, but the shared printer shelf is open, and printed pages can sit there for several minutes. A small notification when a job is finished or a prompt to collect it would be sensible. I have not had anything go missing, and I do not want to suggest that I have had a security problem. This is just a practical concern for client documents.

Overall, I keep coming back because the location is convenient, the desks are comfortable, and the staff are kind. I would make four improvements. First, show room equipment and guest rules in the booking flow. Second, label the early access limits and improve the side gate sign. Third, set a routine for lighting, temperature, and clearing the kitchen. Fourth, make the locker and cancellation rules easier to find. These are modest changes rather than a request to redesign the place. I asked one staff member about the flickering booth light, and she said, “We'll put it on the list,” which was a reasonable response. But it would be helpful to know when reports have been dealt with. With those details improved, Harbor House would work even better for people who need a dependable base for a few hours rather than a permanent office.

last spring i decided to get my uncle's old bicycle working, mostly because it had been leaning against the back wall of my garage for years and i kept moving boxes around it. it was a blue steel touring bike, probably from the late eighties, with a rack over the back wheel and a small bell that still made a sound. my uncle had given it to me when he moved, but i had never ridden it. the tires were flat, the chain looked orange in places, and the right brake lever pulled nearly to the handlebar. i assumed it would need a quick pump and maybe some oil, which was not a very informed assumption.

I started by trying to turn the pedals while the bike was on its kickstand. The rear wheel moved a little, then stopped with a clunk. I turned it backwards and heard a dry scraping noise that seemed to come from the derailleur. I decided the derailleur was bent, although i did not know how to check that properly. When i looked closer, the rear wheel was sitting slightly crooked between the frame tubes. One side of the axle was not all the way down in its slot. I loosened the nuts, pushed the wheel into place, and tightened them again with a wrench from the kitchen drawer. The wheel turned more freely after that. The clunk did not disappear altogether, but it was quieter, so i thought i had found the main problem.

I took the bike to a repair shop to ask whether the frame was worth working on. The mechanic looked at the frame and said it seemed sound, but the tires were too old to trust and the brake cables were frayed near the levers. He also pointed at the chain and said it was stretched, though he didn't measure it in front of me. He gave me a rough estimate of about $180 if they did the tires, cables, chain, and a tune-up. I thanked him and took the bike home because i wanted to understand what the parts cost and whether i could do some of it. My neighbor Elena, who keeps two bikes in her front hallway, said i should take pictures before removing anything and write down the cable routing. She also said not to buy a chain until i checked the old one with a chain gauge. I had not known a chain gauge existed.

At a hardware store and a bike shop, i put together a list on my phone. Two tires and tubes came to $78, a pair of brake cables and housing was $24, and a chain was $22. The chain gauge i borrowed from Elena showed that the chain was worn past the mark on the tool. I also bought new brake pads for $18 because the old ones had hard, shiny surfaces and small cracks. I could have saved money by reusing the tubes, but one had a patch near the valve and the other had a bulge when i inflated it. I didn't want to trust either one on a ride. I left the rear rack and the bell alone because they were both still attached and seemed usable. The total for parts was more than i expected, but still less than the shop estimate, even before labor.

Replacing the tires was the first job that felt straightforward. I got the front tire off with plastic levers and found a strip of cloth tape inside the rim, with one frayed edge. I replaced it with rim tape from the bike shop. The rear tire took longer because i kept pinching the tube between the tire and the rim, and had to let the air out twice to fix it. After both tires were on, i inflated them to the pressure printed on the sidewalls, 65 psi. The wheels looked round when i spun them, though i could see a slight side-to-side wobble in the rear one. I wrote that down instead of trying to straighten it myself, because i had no spoke wrench and did not know which spokes to adjust.

The brake cable replacement was where my confidence went ahead of my skill. I took a picture of the front brake first, then cut the new housing to what looked like the same length. I did not leave enough extra at the turn near the fork. When i pulled the lever, the cable moved, but it dragged and the lever did not spring back quickly. Elena came over to look, and she noticed the housing end had not been cut square. She let me use a small cable cutter and showed me how to seat the metal end caps. The front brake worked better after that. On the rear brake, i put the cable through the wrong side of the pinch bolt, so pulling the lever made the pads rub unevenly. I loosened it and rerouted it, but by then i had spent most of the afternoon on one cable. I was annoyed, especially because the job had looked simple in a video.

I changed the chain the next day. I counted the links on the old one before removing it and matched the new chain length to that count. That seemed less confusing than trying to judge length from the bike. The chain tool pushed out the old pin cleanly, but i struggled to connect the new chain without twisting it. Once it was on, i turned the pedals by hand and shifted through the gears. The chain jumped once on the smallest rear cog. I checked the wheel again and found it was not quite centered after i had taken it out to replace the tire. I loosened the axle nuts and reseated it. The jump happened less often, but did not stop every time. I decided not to adjust the derailleur without somebody showing me what each screw did.

Before riding, i checked the brake pads against the rims, squeezed both levers hard, and walked the bike forward while holding each brake separately. The front wheel stopped; the rear stopped too, although its lever still came closer to the handlebar than i wanted. I checked that the axle nuts were tight, that the tires held air, and that the pedals did not feel loose. I also looked for tools and leftover parts on the floor, then took a short loop around the block instead of heading for the longer path by the river. The first few minutes felt unfamiliar because the handlebars were lower than on my newer bike. The bell worked, and the gears shifted well enough on the flat streets. On a small hill, the chain skipped once when i pressed hard on the pedals, so i eased off and walked the last part.

When i got back, i checked the brakes again and felt the rims for heat, though they were cool. I noticed the rear tire had lost a little air, but i couldn't tell whether it was from the valve or because i had not tightened the pump head properly. I pumped it up again and left the bike overnight. In the morning it still felt firm. I spent $142 on the parts, not counting the chain gauge Elena lent me or the tools i borrowed. The shop's estimate still might have been worth paying for, especially if the shifting needed more attention, but doing the work myself showed me which parts were old and where my own mistakes happened. I learned that a small visual clue, like the crooked wheel, can matter more than the problem i first imagine. I also learned that the bike could be ridden around the block, but that the skipped chain and close rear brake lever were still there in my mind as i put it back in the garage.

i booked the Old Quay history walk on a Tuesday evening, mostly because the listing said it covered the mill lane and the old ferry steps, which are places i have walked past for years without knowing much about them. The booking page was a little awkward on my phone. The date selector kept jumping back to the current month, and i had to enter my email twice because the first time it looked like nothing had happened. A confirmation arrived after a few minutes, though, and it had the meeting point written clearly as the clock outside the market hall. There was no reminder on the day, which was fine, but the page did not say whether the tour went ahead in heavy rain, so i wasn't sure what to expect when the forecast changed.

It was raining lightly when we met, then getting colder as the evening went on. There were eleven of us, plus Mara, our guide. She had a folder with old street maps in it and spoke in a relaxed way, not like she was reciting a script, although now and then she had to stop and check a date. We began beside the market hall clock, which is not the original clock, apparently, but a replacement installed after the face was damaged. Mara said, “The clock has told the right time less often than you’d think.” I couldn't tell whether she meant that as a joke about this particular clock or about the town in general. She also pointed out a narrow line of darker stone near the corner and said it might mark where the earlier market wall stood. She was careful to say that the line could have another explanation, and that there is no surviving plan that settles it.

From there we walked down Bell Street toward the river. The first problem with the route came almost immediately: the pavement narrows outside the pharmacy, and a delivery van was parked partly across it. We had to go into the road for a short stretch, and the group bunched up behind Mara because there wasn't much space to pass. A person using a walking stick was with us and managed it, but it did not look comfortable. Mara waited on the other side and checked that everyone had crossed before she carried on. There are also two high kerbs before the river path, with no dropped section at the second one. I don't know if the route is always this difficult or if the van made it unusually awkward that evening, but it would be worth asking before booking if steps and uneven pavement are a concern.

At the old ferry steps, the stones were slick from rain. We stayed at the top rather than going down, which was probably sensible. Mara said the ferry landing was probably in use by the early eighteenth century, though the records she had seen were incomplete and some of the dates came from later references. “People tend to give the ferry a birthday it never had,” she said. She explained that the river edge used to be closer to the warehouses, but then added, “The river used to come farther in, or at least people say it did.” I liked that she marked the difference between what the documents show and what local accounts repeat. She showed us a small iron ring set into the wall and said it may have been used to tie boats, but she did not present that as certain. The group stayed there for about ten minutes, and it was difficult to hear her when a bus went by on the road above us.

The next stop was Mill Lane, which is now a short row of houses and a takeaway, not much of a lane in the sense i had imagined. Mara had brought a photograph showing the mill buildings before they were demolished. We compared the old roofline with the modern one across the street, although the angle of the photograph made that harder than it sounds. She said one building in the picture might have been a counting room, but she wasn't sure because its use is not identified in the caption. I appreciated that she did not turn every blank space in the record into a confident story. She did say the mill employed local families, but couldn't give a number, and said the surviving lists were mostly for people who rented rooms rather than everyone working there. At this stop we were standing on a sloping pavement, and there was nowhere nearby to sit. The talk went on for a while, so one person leaned against the takeaway window ledge, which looked a bit uncomfortable for them.

A closed gate blocked the planned route toward the old rope yard. Mara checked her map, then took us through the public garden on the next street and around the back of the library. It added maybe eight minutes, and the garden was a genuinely helpful detour rather than just a way to get us back on schedule. There was a low stone boundary there that she thought might have been reused from a rope-yard wall, but she said it could also have come from a later garden project. The detour was quieter than the road, and there were benches, though they were wet. The path has gravel and a shallow slope; it should be manageable for some people with mobility issues, but it isn't smooth, and a wheelchair user could find the turn by the library tight. Mara checked with the group before using the narrow section and offered the option of waiting by the gate, but nobody took it.

Near the library she talked about a fire that damaged several buildings in the 1840s. The local account she had read puts the fire in 1846, while a newspaper notice she showed us appears to say 1847. She did not know whether one of those dates was a printing error or whether the accounts were describing separate incidents. The notice also says that a store of rope was lost, but not exactly where it had been kept. Mara said, “I think the story got tidier each time it was retold.” That seemed fair, although she didn't explain how she had traced the retellings. By then the rain had picked up, and she held the paper under her coat while we looked at the copy. The old library itself is still used, but the entrance has a short flight of steps and I didn't see a ramp from where we stood. We did not go inside.

The last stop was the small stone plaque at the corner of Anchor Square. We stood under an awning from a closed shop while Mara talked about the square's name. She said it may refer to a storage yard for ship fittings, but she had not found a map showing an anchor yard there. The plaque names two people involved in a dock petition; one of them, she said, was a shopkeeper who argued against extending the toll. She described the petition as one of the reasons the quay road was widened, then corrected herself and said it was one factor mentioned in a council note, not necessarily the reason. That kind of mid-sentence adjustment happened a few times, and i found it more reassuring than annoying. The tour finished roughly when the booking page had said it would, about an hour and three quarters after we started.

I came away with a better sense of how close the market, mill lane, ferry landing, and quay were to one another, and with a handful of questions i hadn't had before. I also had cold hands, damp shoes, and a few stretches where the group was difficult to hear over traffic. The walk is interesting if you like small uncertainties and ordinary street details as much as dates and named buildings. I would recommend it to someone comfortable with uneven pavement who doesn't mind standing outside in poor weather; for someone who needs a smooth, step-free route, i would ask Mara about the current path before paying, especially while the gate by the rope yard is closed.

The room had twelve desktop computers and six loan laptops, and the laptops were supposed to connect to the guest network. On the first evening, the network password printed on the booking sheet did not work, and the centre’s evening supervisor had gone home before I noticed. Three laptops eventually connected through a phone hotspot, but that was not allowed for the whole class, so students shared screens in pairs. I had downloaded the editor installer onto a USB stick, but two computers blocked it because the user accounts did not have permission. We used the browser editor instead. It worked, although saving a project required making an account, and I had not included that step in my setup notes.

That meant the first exercise, which was meant to be a quick change from printing “Hello, world!” to printing each student’s name, took nearly the whole first hour. One student had typed the quotation marks as two apostrophes, and the program gave an error that was hard to explain without first explaining what a string was. Another student got the message right but had put the name outside the quotation marks. I went round the room, but I was also trying to help people log in and find the run button. One student said, “I thought computers were meant to do what you tell them.” I thought it was a funny comment, though by the end I wondered if the exercise had asked for too much setup and too little programming.

For the second meeting I moved the login instructions to the beginning of the handout and put a sample account on the whiteboard, but I did not use the sample account myself before class. It turned out that the browser editor had changed its sign-in screen. I showed students how to use the editor without saving, and we got through a short exercise with variables for a snack order. They chose a drink and a price, then changed the values and predicted what the program would print. Several students understood the prediction part before they understood why the variable name could be used later. I may have explained that distinction too quickly. One person started writing the whole order as one long print statement, which did work, and I did not want to frame that as wrong when the point was only to see a value change.

In week three, we used if statements to decide whether a made-up bus fare should be full price or half price. I had written the conditions on the board, but I had accidentally used “age < 16” in one example and “age <= 16” in the next, without saying why the boundary had changed. A student noticed and asked whether a person who was exactly sixteen paid the full fare. I said that depended on the rules we were modelling, but I could see that I had made it look like a Python issue rather than a choice in the example. We changed the rule together and tested ages fifteen, sixteen, and seventeen. That was a useful moment, although I think the class was more interested in whether the fare policy was fair than in the symbols, and I had not planned enough time for that conversation.

I tried to include different ways of following the lesson because the group did not all work at the same pace. I handed out printed copies of the examples as well as putting them on the projector, and I used a larger font after one student told me the code was difficult to read from the back. I also started saying the punctuation aloud while typing, but I found that saying “open parenthesis, close parenthesis” made me speak so slowly that I lost track of what I was explaining. After class, I asked the student whether the printed copies helped; they said, “The paper is good because I can circle the bit you mean.” I took that as a reason to keep the handouts, but it might not have been the font alone that made the lesson easier to follow.

I had not been sure whether the space would be useful, but the student later showed me a copy with notes written between the steps and said it was easier to keep their place. I did not ask for more details about why, and I did not want to assume that one adjustment would suit everyone. I showed a version using a for loop, and one student asked why we could not just write five print lines. Those requests point in different directions, and I have not worked out how to balance them.

Two students could not attend on Saturdays, so I emailed them the handout and a short recording of the demonstration. I do not know whether they watched the recording, and I did not want to make attendance sound compulsory when I sent it. I shortened the review to make time for the exercise, but then the students who had missed the Saturday meeting had less chance to ask questions. I gave them a starter file and allowed them to use the handouts, but asked them to explain one choice they made. One student asked whether they could submit a photo of handwritten code because their home computer was shared with family. I marked the task with notes on what each program did, rather than a score, but I did not explain that plan clearly before they started.

Two asked for more time on errors, and one said they would have liked to build something larger over several weeks instead of doing separate exercises. A student wrote, “I didn’t feel stupid when it broke, which is not what I expected.” I was glad to read that, but I do not know whether it was because of the classroom atmosphere, the handouts, or the way I handled mistakes. I also wonder whether my habit of fixing errors at the front of the room made it seem as though I could always see the answer quickly, even when I was figuring it out as I went.

For another course, I would ask the centre to test the network, account access, and installed software before the first evening, and I would bring a no-login version of the exercises in case that still failed. I would keep the printed instructions and send them in advance, but I might make the font size and spacing options more explicit. I would also like to keep the student choice of trying a written list or a diagram, although I need to check whether preparing both is manageable. I do not know whether the answer is fewer topics, longer meetings, or a different rhythm of demonstration and practice. Would a course that met once a week give students more time to try things between sessions, or would they lose the thread? And how can I find out which changes helped without asking students to do more work just to explain the course to me?
